rounds.text: Marushika Technology Ltd exhibits compelling undervaluation, trading at a P/E of just 8.26x against a sector benchmark of 20.15x, alongside a discounted EV/EBITDA of 5.16x compared to the sector's 10.8x [E1, E6, E11]. This modest multiple is paired with exceptional operational efficiency, highlighted by a trailing twelve-month compounded sales growth of 37% and profit growth of 43%, substantially outpacing sector medians of 14.8% and 10.3% respectively [E14, E15, E50, E49]. Furthermore, the company generates elite returns, posting a robust ROCE of 34.26% and an ROE of 28.57%, both vastly outperforming their respective sector benchmarks [E10, E9]. Institutional confidence is underscored by a positive money flow and rising domestic institutional ownership to 8.55% [E31, E30]. Finally, the reverse DCF reveals that the current market price implies an unrealistic negative earnings growth of -4.5%, completely disconnecting from the business's actual multi-year upward trajectory [E34, E45, E46]. Conceded: the dividend yield stands at 0.00% and free cash flow was negative at Rs -5 Cr in Mar 2026 due to extended working capital days [E4, E23, E41].

Marushika Technology Ltd carries severe underlying cash generation and working capital risks that undermine its reported earnings quality [E21, E40, E41]. Despite claiming robust profits, the company exhibits a dismal cash conversion ratio of just 0.22x against reported profit for March 2026, meaning profits are running far ahead of actual cash collected due to receivables and accruals [E21]. This disconnect is further evidenced by a negative free cash flow of Rs -5 Cr in March 2026 alongside ballooning debt, with borrowings doubling from Rs 7 Cr to Rs 16 Cr by September 2026 [E23, E26]. Operational efficiency is also deteriorating rapidly, highlighted by exceptionally high debtor days of 182 and a near-doubling of working capital days from 60.5 days to 112 days [E40, E41]. Furthermore, shareholders receive zero return in cash, as evidenced by a 0.00% dividend yield despite the reporting of repeated profits [E4, E39]. Conceded: the company demonstrates high historical returns on equity, strong short-term liquidity with a current ratio of 2.03x, and positive institutional money flow [E13, E25, E31].

Conceded: cash conversion is low at 0.22x and free cash flow is negative at Rs -5 Cr [E21, E23], alongside high debtor days of 182 and an increase in working capital days to 112 [E40, E41]. Conceded: borrowings rose from Rs 7 Cr to Rs 16 Cr [E26] and dividend yield is 0.00% [E4]. However, these capital allocations and working capital dynamics do not negate the company's elite core profitability, demonstrated by a stellar ROCE of 34.26% and ROE of 28.57%, both drastically outperforming sector benchmarks of 11.63% and 10.05% [E10, E9]. Furthermore, despite the headline debt increase, the overall leverage remains conservatively financed with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.29x alongside a comfortable short-term current ratio of 2.03x [E24, E25]. The market is excessively penalizing the stock for temporary working capital friction while ignoring a robust 37% compounded sales growth and 43% compounded profit growth [E14, E15]. Finally, domestic institutions are actively backing this fundamental strength, increasing their holding by 0.95 percentage points to drive positive institutional money flow [E30, E31].

Conceded: ROCE is 34.26% and ROE is 28.57% [E10, E9], debt-to-equity is 0.29x alongside a current ratio of 2.03x [E24, E25], sales and profit growth are 37% and 43% [E14, E15], and domestic institutions increased holdings by 0.95 percentage points [E30]. However, citing these figures ignores the severe operational reality that profits are entirely detached from actual cash generation, evidenced by a dismal cash conversion ratio of 0.22x and negative free cash flow of Rs -5 Cr in Mar 2026 [E21, E23]. This shortfall directly stems from ballooning collection friction, with high debtors reaching 182 days and working capital days surging from 60.5 to 112 days [E40, E41]. Furthermore, despite being called conservative, borrowings more than doubled from Rs 7 Cr to Rs 16 Cr within a single year [E26], while the company refuses to return any capital to shareholders, maintaining a 0.00% dividend yield [E4]. Finally, the institutional picture is mixed rather than uniformly supportive, as foreign institutions actively reduced their holdings by 0.59 percentage points [E29].
